summary: Describes the link bundling construct in GMPLS signaling for cases where a link identifier plus label cannot unambiguously identify the resource used by a path. It updates the interface identification TLVs. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4201 defines how GMPLS can group several component links into one advertised traffic-engineering link. Routing can use the group, while signaling identifies the particular component link and label needed by an LSP.

questions: what is link bundling in mpls te
how is bandwidth advertised for a bundled link
subtitle: How GMPLS groups component links for routing while signaling still identifies the exact resource used by an LSP.

tldr.problem: For some GMPLS links, a link identifier and label do not uniquely identify the physical resource used by a Label Switched Path.
tldr.mechanism: A TE link is divided into component links, each with a node-unique identifier. Routing advertises the bundle, while signaling names the component link and label.
tldr.outcome: Bundling reduces routing information while preserving resource identification for signaling. RFC 4201 updates RFC 3471, RFC 3472, and RFC 3473 and deprecates two Interface_ID TLV types.

facts.value: At least one component link is alive

facts.label: Maximum Bandwidth
facts.value: Not used; Maximum LSP Bandwidth replaces it

today: RFC 4201 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It updates RFC 3471, RFC 3472, and RFC 3473; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Bundle Traffic-Engineering Links
sections.content:
A traffic-engineering (TE) link represents physical resources between label switching routers for path computation and GMPLS signaling. In some cases a TE link identifier and label are enough to identify the resource used by a Label Switched Path (LSP). In other cases they are not.

The RFC gives the example of several fibers between SONET/SDH cross-connects. A time-slot label has meaning only within one fiber, so signaling must also identify the fiber. Link bundling divides the TE link's resources into disjoint component links so that a component-link identifier plus a label identifies a resource. Advertising the bundle instead of every component also reduces the information OSPF or IS-IS must handle.
sections.plainLanguage: A single link label does not always identify a resource precisely enough. Link bundling groups resources for routing but keeps component identifiers available to signaling.

sections.title: Component Links and Bundled Links
sections.content:
The resources in a TE link are partitioned into minimal, disjoint subsets. Each subset is a component link, and the complete TE link is the bundled link. A component-link identifier must be unique for the node, so the pair of component-link identifier and label identifies the resource used by an LSP.

Both ends of the bundled link must partition resources consistently and understand each other's component-link identifiers. Component links can be numbered or unnumbered. The bundled link can independently be numbered or unnumbered.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle contains component links, each with an identifier unique on its node. Both ends must agree on the partition and understand the identifiers used by the other end.

sections.title: Restrictions and Link Liveness
sections.content:
All component links in a bundle must have the same Link Type, TE metric, and resource classes at each end. They must connect the same pair of label switching routers. For multi-access links, the connected routers and Designated Router must be the same on each component link; otherwise those links must not be bundled.

A bundled link is alive when at least one component link is alive. Liveness may be determined using IS-IS or OSPF hellos, RSVP Hello, LMP hellos, or layer 1 or layer 2 indications. Once the bundle is alive, it can be advertised as a TE link and its information flooded.
sections.plainLanguage: Component links must meet the RFC's matching rules before they can share a bundle. The bundle remains available while at least one of its component links is alive.

sections.title: Identifying the Component During Signaling
sections.content:
Routing advertises the bundled link, not its component links. The choice of component link is therefore local to the two routers at the ends of the bundle. The sender of a Path or REQUEST message chooses the component link; for a bidirectional LSP, a component link is chosen in each direction.

Component-link identifiers are carried in RSVP or CR-LDP messages. Interface Identification TLV types 1, 2, and 3 SHOULD be used for IPv4 numbered, IPv6 numbered, and unnumbered component links. Types 4 and 5 SHOULD NOT be used. For a unidirectional LSP, one TLV SHOULD identify the downstream component. For a bidirectional LSP, one or two TLVs identify downstream and upstream components; one TLV can identify both.

If the same label is valid on every component, two TLVs SHOULD be used: one for the bundle and one with the bundle-scope value 0xFFFFFFFF. When an error occurs, received TLVs SHOULD be copied into the corresponding RSVP or CR-LDP error information.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender chooses a component link and includes its identifier in signaling. When a label applies across the whole bundle, a special value identifies that scope.

sections.title: Advertising and Reserving Bandwidth
sections.content:
The bundle's Link Type, TE metric, and resource classes come from its component links. Maximum Reservable Bandwidth is the sum across components, as is Unreserved Bandwidth at a given priority. Maximum Bandwidth is not used for a bundled link; Maximum LSP Bandwidth at a priority is the maximum value among its component links.

Admission control is performed for each component. An LSP requiring bandwidth b at setup priority p fits if at least one component has Maximum LSP Bandwidth of at least b at priority p. If several components fit, the implementation chooses one. When a component goes down, its unreserved bandwidth becomes zero and the bundle's values are recalculated. If all components are down, the bundle MUST NOT be advertised into OSPF or IS-IS.
sections.plainLanguage: Some bandwidth values are added across the component links, while the largest single-component limit determines whether one LSP can fit. Admission control selects a component that can carry the LSP.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4201 reuses procedures defined in other specifications and says it raises no new security issues for RSVP-TE or CR-LDP beyond those documents.

The RFC updates the recommended usage in the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry. Interface_ID type 4, COMPONENT_IF_DOWNSTREAM, and type 5, COMPONENT_IF_UPSTREAM, are marked DEPRECATED.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says it adds no new security issues beyond the signaling procedures it uses. It marks two older component-interface TLV types as deprecated.
